claim: Chlamydia trachomatis alternates between two functional forms during its developmental cycle: elementary body (EB) and reticulate body (RB).
source: The obligate intracellular bacterium Chlamydia alternates between two functional forms during its developmental cycle: elementary body (EB) and reticulate body (RB).
evidence: This is a well-established characteristic of Chlamydia described in the abstract and supported by citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: The molecular mechanisms governing the transitions between EB and RB forms are unknown.
source: However, the molecular mechanisms governing the transitions between these forms are unknown.
evidence: This statement is made in the abstract and represents the knowledge gap that the study addresses.

claim: Cyclic di-AMP (c-di-AMP) is a key factor in triggering the transition from RB to EB (secondary differentiation) in the chlamydial developmental cycle.
source: Here, we present evidence that cyclic di-AMP (c-di-AMP) is a key factor in triggering the transition from RB to EB (i.e., secondary differentiation) in the chlamydial developmental cycle.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by multiple experimental approaches including genetic manipulation, c-di-AMP measurements, and phenotypic analyses.

claim: Increases in c-di-AMP resulted in an earlier increase in transcription of EB-associated genes.
source: Increases in c-di-AMP resulted in an earlier increase in transcription of EB-associated genes, and this was further manifested in earlier production of EBs.
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data showing increased hctA transcripts at 14 hpi in strains overproducing c-di-AMP, and RNA sequencing data showing upregulation of late genes.

claim: Increases in c-di-AMP resulted in earlier production of EBs.
source: Increases in c-di-AMP resulted in an earlier increase in transcription of EB-associated genes, and this was further manifested in earlier production of EBs.
evidence: This is supported by IFU assays showing higher EB yields at 18 and 20 hpi in the dacAop overexpression strain.

claim: When c-di-AMP levels were decreased, developmental cycle progression was delayed.
source: In contrast, when c-di-AMP levels were decreased, developmental cycle progression was delayed.
evidence: This is supported by data from the dacA-KD strain showing reduced IFUs, decreased late gene transcripts, and delayed EB production.

claim: There is a threshold level of c-di-AMP needed to trigger secondary differentiation in Chlamydia.
source: Based on these data, we conclude there is a threshold level of c-di-AMP needed to trigger secondary differentiation in Chlamydia.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the observation that c-di-AMP levels increase during the developmental cycle and that manipulating these levels affects the timing of secondary differentiation.

claim: This study identifies a mechanism by which secondary differentiation is initiated in Chlamydia.
source: This study identifies a mechanism by which secondary differentiation is initiated in Chlamydia and reveals a critical role for the second messenger signaling molecule c-di-AMP in this process.
evidence: This is the overarching conclusion of the study based on the experimental data presented.

claim: C-di-AMP plays a critical role in the secondary differentiation process.
source: This study identifies a mechanism by which secondary differentiation is initiated in Chlamydia and reveals a critical role for the second messenger signaling molecule c-di-AMP in this process.
evidence: This is supported by the comprehensive experimental data showing that manipulating c-di-AMP levels directly affects secondary differentiation.

claim: EBs are infectious but non-dividing cells.
source: During this cycle, Chlamydia transitions between two different functional and morphological forms: the elementary body (EB), an infectious but non-dividing cell, and the reticulate body (RB), a dividing but non-infectious cell (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a well-established characteristic of Chlamydia EBs cited from the literature.

claim: RBs are dividing but non-infectious cells.
source: During this cycle, Chlamydia transitions between two different functional and morphological forms: the elementary body (EB), an infectious but non-dividing cell, and the reticulate body (RB), a dividing but non-infectious cell (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a well-established characteristic of Chlamydia RBs cited from the literature.

claim: The intermediate body (IB) is a transitional form from the RB to EB.
source: A third form, the intermediate body (IB) is a transitional form from the RB to EB.
evidence: This is a known characteristic of the chlamydial developmental cycle.

claim: EBs are small (~0.3 μm).
source: For example, EBs are small (~0.3 μm), have a highly disulfide-crosslinked outer membrane (Everett and Hatch, 1991), and have DNA condensed by histone-like proteins (Hackstadt et al., 1991).
evidence: This is a known morphological characteristic of EBs supported by citations.

claim: EBs have a highly disulfide-crosslinked outer membrane.
source: For example, EBs are small (~0.3 μm), have a highly disulfide-crosslinked outer membrane (Everett and Hatch, 1991), and have DNA condensed by histone-like proteins (Hackstadt et al., 1991).
evidence: This is a known characteristic of EBs supported by the citation to Everett and Hatch, 1991.

claim: EBs have DNA condensed by histone-like proteins.
source: For example, EBs are small (~0.3 μm), have a highly disulfide-crosslinked outer membrane (Everett and Hatch, 1991), and have DNA condensed by histone-like proteins (Hackstadt et al., 1991).
evidence: This is a known characteristic of EBs supported by the citation to Hackstadt et al., 1991.

claim: RBs are larger (~1 μm) than EBs.
source: In contrast, RBs are larger (~1 μm), have a Gram-negative cell envelope that lacks peptidoglycan (Moulder, 1993; Fox et al., 1990; Barbour et al., 1982), and have a dispersed chromosome.
evidence: This is a known morphological characteristic of RBs.

claim: RBs have a Gram-negative cell envelope that lacks peptidoglycan.
source: In contrast, RBs are larger (~1 μm), have a Gram-negative cell envelope that lacks peptidoglycan (Moulder, 1993; Fox et al., 1990; Barbour et al., 1982), and have a dispersed chromosome.
evidence: This is a known characteristic of RBs supported by multiple citations.

claim: RBs have a dispersed chromosome.
source: In contrast, RBs are larger (~1 μm), have a Gram-negative cell envelope that lacks peptidoglycan (Moulder, 1993; Fox et al., 1990; Barbour et al., 1982), and have a dispersed chromosome.
evidence: This is a known characteristic of RBs.

claim: RBs divide by an asymmetric polarized division mechanism dependent on MreB-directed peptidoglycan synthesis specifically at the septum.
source: RBs divide by an asymmetric polarized division mechanism dependent on MreB-directed peptidoglycan synthesis specifically at the septum (Abdelrahman et al., 2016; Liechti et al., 2016; Ouellette et al., 2012; Lee et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations describing the division mechanism of RBs.

claim: Chlamydia expresses genes in a temporally defined manner that corresponds broadly with its developmental cycle.
source: Not surprisingly, Chlamydia expresses genes in a temporally defined manner that corresponds broadly with its developmental cycle (Belland et al., 2003; Ouellette et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies characterizing temporal gene expression in Chlamydia.

claim: 'Early' genes (e.g., euo) are expressed immediately upon entry into a target host cell and are likely involved in establishing the intracellular niche of Chlamydia, the inclusion, and mediating primary differentiation from EB to RB.
source: 'Early' genes (e.g., euo) are expressed immediately upon entry into a target host cell and are likely involved in establishing the intracellular niche of Chlamydia, the inclusion, and mediating primary differentiation from EB to RB.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of chlamydial gene expression patterns.

claim: 'Mid' cycle genes (e.g., mreB, clpPX) facilitate RB replication and division and inclusion growth.
source: 'Mid' cycle genes (e.g., mreB, clpPX) facilitate RB replication and division and inclusion growth.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of chlamydial gene expression patterns.

claim: 'Late' genes (e.g. hctA, omcB) are expressed when secondary differentiation is initiated to trigger EB formation.
source: 'Late' genes (e.g. hctA, omcB) are expressed when secondary differentiation is initiated to trigger EB formation.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of chlamydial gene expression patterns.

claim: The signals or events that initiate differentiation from one form to the other are not known.
source: Although developmental gene expression has been characterized for decades, the signals or events that initiate differentiation from one form to the other are not known.
evidence: This statement represents the knowledge gap that the study addresses.

claim: C-di-AMP accumulates over the course of the chlamydial developmental cycle.
source: As part of their study, the authors determined that c-di-AMP accumulates over the course of the chlamydial developmental cycle, that EBs have high levels of this molecule whereas RBs have low levels, and that DacA is a diadenylate cyclase.
evidence: This is based on the findings from Barker et al., 2013, and confirmed by the authors' own measurements.

claim: EBs have high levels of c-di-AMP whereas RBs have low levels.
source: As part of their study, the authors determined that c-di-AMP accumulates over the course of the chlamydial developmental cycle, that EBs have high levels of this molecule whereas RBs have low levels, and that DacA is a diadenylate cyclase.
evidence: This is based on the findings from Barker et al., 2013, and confirmed by the authors' own measurements showing higher c-di-AMP at 24 hpi compared to 16 hpi.

claim: DacA is a diadenylate cyclase.
source: As part of their study, the authors determined that c-di-AMP accumulates over the course of the chlamydial developmental cycle, that EBs have high levels of this molecule whereas RBs have low levels, and that DacA is a diadenylate cyclase.
evidence: This is based on the findings from Barker et al., 2013.

claim: C-di-AMP is implicated in the response to changes in osmotic pressure in Gram-positive bacteria.
source: For example, c-di-AMP is implicated in the response to changes in osmotic pressure.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations describing c-di-AMP function in other bacteria.

claim: C-di-AMP binds to proteins associated with K+ uptake systems such as Ktr/Trk, KimA, Kup, and Kdp and inhibits their activities in Bacillus subtilis, Staphylococcus aureus, and Lactococcus lactis.
source: In these mechanisms, c-di-AMP binds to proteins associated with K+ uptake systems such as Ktr/Trk, KimA, Kup, and Kdp and inhibits their activities in Bacillus subtilis, Staphylococcus aureus, and Lactococcus lactis (Kim et al., 2015; Gibhardt et al., 2019; Quintana et al., 2019; Moscoso et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations describing c-di-AMP function in other bacteria.

claim: The cation/proton antiporter A (CpaA) is activated by binding c-di-AMP in S. aureus.
source: In S. aureus, the cation/proton antiporter A (CpaA) is activated by binding c-di-AMP (Corrigan et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by the citation to Corrigan et al., 2013.

claim: C-di-AMP binds to the riboswitch upstream of the genes encoding the K+ transporters and controls their transcriptional levels.
source: Moreover, c-di-AMP binds to the riboswitch upstream of the genes encoding the K+ transporters and controls their transcriptional levels (Wang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by the citation to Wang et al., 2019.

claim: Chlamydia lacks annotated orthologs of K+ transporters.
source: Of note, Chlamydia lacks annotated orthologs of K+ transporters.
evidence: This is based on genomic analysis of Chlamydia.

claim: C-di-AMP has been reported to affect DNA replication and sporulation.
source: In addition to osmotic homeostasis, c-di-AMP has been reported to affect DNA replication and sporulation (Bejerano-Sagie et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by the citation to Bejerano-Sagie et al., 2006.

claim: When DNA damage is detected, DisA, a diadenylate cyclase, forms a DNA repair complex with RecA and RadA, resulting in inhibition of diadenylate cyclase activity in B. subtilis.
source: When DNA damage is detected, DisA, a diadenylate cyclase, forms a DNA repair complex with RecA and RadA, resulting in inhibition of diadenylate cyclase activity in B. subtilis.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations describing c-di-AMP function in B. subtilis.

claim: C. trachomatis only encodes the synthesis mechanism for c-di-AMP as it possesses the genes for diadenylate cyclase (dacA) and its regulator (ybbR) within a bicistronic operon, but no annotated PDEs or c-di-AMP transporters.
source: Interestingly, C. trachomatis only encodes the synthesis mechanism as it possesses the genes for diadenylate cyclase (dacA) and its regulator (ybbR) within a bicistronic operon, but no annotated PDEs or c-di-AMP transporters (Stephens et al., 1998).
evidence: This is based on genomic analysis of C. trachomatis supported by the citation to Stephens et al., 1998.

claim: Both DacA and YbbR are predicted to contain transmembrane domains (3 for DacA and 1 for YbbR).
source: Both DacA and YbbR are predicted to contain transmembrane domains (3 for DacA and 1 for YbbR) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1; Barker et al., 2013).
evidence: This is based on computational prediction using TOPCONS and supported by the citation to Barker et al., 2013.

claim: C-di-AMP levels were significantly higher at 24 hpi (~1700 pg/mL) compared to 16 hpi (~250 pg/mL) and increased approximately sevenfold over this timeframe.
source: We observed that c-di-AMP levels were significantly higher at 24 hpi (~1700 pg/mL) compared to 16 hpi (~250 pg/mL) and increased approximately sevenfold over this timeframe (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is based on ELISA measurements of c-di-AMP levels shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The concentration of c-di-AMP in the culture conditions necessary to trigger conversion of RBs to EBs is at most 1700 pg/mL.
source: From these data, we infer that the concentration of c-di-AMP in our culture conditions necessary to trigger conversion of RBs to EBs is at most 1700 pg/mL.
evidence: This is an inference based on the c-di-AMP measurements at 24 hpi when EBs are being produced.

claim: Overexpressing DacA resulted in ~ fourfold increase in c-di-AMP levels as compared to the mCherry-expressing strain at 16 hpi (~1,000 pg/mL) and ~ threefold increase at 24 hpi (~5000 pg/mL).
source: Overexpressing DacA resulted in ~ fourfold increase in c-di-AMP levels as compared to the mCherry-expressing strain at 16 hpi (~1,000 pg/mL) and ~ threefold increase at 24 hpi (~5000 pg/mL).
evidence: This is based on ELISA measurements of c-di-AMP levels shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Overexpressing YbbR_6xH did not impact c-di-AMP production.
source: Overexpressing YbbR_6xH did not impact c-di-AMP production.
evidence: This is based on ELISA measurements of c-di-AMP levels shown in Figure 1E.

claim: When overexpressing the catalytically inactive mutant of DacA(D164N), c-di-AMP levels were ~ twofold lower at 16 hpi (~115 pg/mL) and, at 24 hpi (~320 pg/mL), was similar to the 16 hpi mCherry control, indicating a severe reduction in c-di-AMP accumulation.
source: When overexpressing the catalytically inactive mutant of DacA(D164N), c-di-AMP levels were ~ twofold lower at 16 hpi (~115 pg/mL) and, at 24 hpi (~320 pg/mL), was similar to the 16 hpi mCherry control, indicating a severe reduction in c-di-AMP accumulation.
evidence: This is based on ELISA measurements of c-di-AMP levels shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Overexpressing ΔTMDacA phenocopied the effect of overexpressing full-length DacA on c-di-AMP production.
source: Overexpressing ΔTMDacA phenocopied the effect of overexpressing full-length DacA on c-di-AMP production.
evidence: This is based on ELISA measurements of c-di-AMP levels shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The negative effects of overexpressing full-length DacA(D164N) associated with reduced c-di-AMP levels were lost when expressing ΔTMDacA(D164N), which phenocopied the mCherry-expressing control.
source: Interestingly, the negative effects of overexpressing full-length DacA(D164N) associated with reduced c-di-AMP levels were lost when expressing ΔTMDacA(D164N), which phenocopied the mCherry-expressing control.
evidence: This is based on ELISA measurements of c-di-AMP levels shown in Figure 1E.

claim: When DacA and YbbR_6xH were co-overexpressed, c-di-AMP levels increased by approximately 30-fold at 16 hpi (~8000 pg/mL) and 120-fold at 24 hpi (~340,000 pg/mL) compared to that of the mCherry-expressing control strain.
source: When DacA and YbbR_6xH were co-overexpressed, c-di-AMP levels increased by approximately 30-fold at 16 hpi (~8000 pg/mL) and 120-fold at 24 hpi (~340,000 pg/mL) compared to that of the mCherry-expressing control strain.
evidence: This is based on ELISA measurements of c-di-AMP levels shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The levels of c-di-AMP at 16 hpi in the dacAop strain (~8000 pg/mL) were higher even than the control strain at 24 hpi (~1700 pg/mL).
source: Of note, the levels of c-di-AMP at 16 hpi in the dacAop strain (~8000 pg/mL) were higher even than the control strain at 24 hpi (~1700 pg/mL; EB threshold in Figure 1E).
evidence: This is based on ELISA measurements of c-di-AMP levels shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Co-overexpressing DacA(D164N) and YbbR_6xH (dacAopMut) resulted in c-di-AMP levels reduced compared to the control at 16 (~100 pg/mL) and 24 hpi (~400 pg/mL), suggesting that c-di-AMP synthase activity was blocked in this strain.
source: Here, c-di-AMP levels were reduced compared to the control at 16 (~100 pg/mL) and 24 hpi (~400 pg/mL), suggesting that c-di-AMP synthase activity was blocked in this strain similar to overexpressing the DacA(D164N) alone.
evidence: This is based on ELISA measurements of c-di-AMP levels shown in Figure 1E.

claim: For the dacA-KD strain, the c-di-AMP level was unchanged at 16 hpi and reduced a statistically significant ~ fivefold at 24 hpi (~500 pg/mL).
source: For the dacA-KD strain, the c-di-AMP level was unchanged at 16 hpi and reduced a statistically significant ~ fivefold at 24 hpi (~500 pg/mL; roughly twice the level of the 16 hr mCherry-expressing control but below the EB threshold).
evidence: This is based on ELISA measurements of c-di-AMP levels shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The loss of c-di-AMP production in the dacA-KD strain was restored in the complemented dacA-KDcom strain, which showed a phenotype similar to the dacAop overexpression strain with c-di-AMP levels above the EB threshold at both timepoints assessed (~3700 pg/mL at 16 hpi;~10,000 pg/mL at 24 hpi).
source: The loss of c-di-AMP production in this strain was restored in the complemented dacA-KDcom strain, which showed a phenotype similar to the dacAop overexpression strain with c-di-AMP levels above the EB threshold at both timepoints assessed (~3700 pg/mL at 16 hpi;~10,000 pg/mL at 24 hpi).
evidence: This is based on ELISA measurements of c-di-AMP levels shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Both DacA and YbbR are necessary for optimal c-di-AMP synthesis in Chlamydia.
source: Based on these data, we conclude that both DacA and YbbR are necessary for optimal c-di-AMP synthesis in Chlamydia.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the observation that co-overexpression of DacA and YbbR resulted in much higher c-di-AMP levels than overexpression of either alone.

claim: Both DacA and YbbR localized at the bacterial membrane.
source: We observed that both DacA and YbbR localized at the bacterial membrane as expected (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on immunofluorescence assay (IFA) images shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: When DacA was overexpressed, the inclusion size was significantly reduced in area (~ sixfold) with larger individual organisms (~ twofold) than those in the uninduced control.
source: When DacA was overexpressed, the inclusion size was significantly reduced in area (~ sixfold) with larger individual organisms (~ twofold) than those in the uninduced control (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on quantification of inclusion area and cell diameter shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Overexpressing the inactive DacA(D164N) mutant resulted in smaller inclusions similar to overexpressing wild-type DacA.
source: Similarly, overexpressing the inactive DacA(D164N) mutant resulted in smaller inclusions similar to overexpressing wild-type DacA (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is based on IFA images and quantification shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: At 24 hpi, both IFUs and genome copy numbers were significantly decreased in the DacA overexpression strain.
source: At 24 hpi, both IFUs and genome copy numbers were significantly decreased in the DacA overexpression strain (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: This is based on IFU assays and qPCR measurements shown in Figure 2C and D.

claim: Overexpression of DacA(D164N) also negatively affected IFU production and resulted in reduced genome copy numbers even though c-di-AMP levels were reduced under these conditions.
source: Like overexpression of the wild-type DacA, overexpression of DacA(D164N) also negatively affected IFU production and resulted in reduced genome copy numbers even though c-di-AMP levels were reduced under these conditions (Figure 2E and F).
evidence: This is based on IFU assays and qPCR measurements shown in Figure 2E and F.

claim: YbbR_6xH overexpression resulted in a statistically significant, ~ twofold decrease in IFU production.
source: YbbR_6xH overexpression did result in a statistically significant, ~ twofold decrease in IFU production (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is based on IFU assays shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: No differences were noted in genome copy number when overexpressing YbbR_6xH.
source: No differences were noted in genome copy number when overexpressing YbbR_6xH (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is based on qPCR measurements shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Overexpression of DacA resulted in elevated euo transcripts and a reduction in the amounts of the late gene transcripts at 24 hpi.
source: Consistent with the genome copy numbers and IFU data, overexpression of DacA resulted in elevated euo transcripts and a reduction in the amounts of the late gene transcripts at 24 hpi (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is based on RT-qPCR measurements shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Similar effects on transcripts were noted when overexpressing DacA(D164N).
source: Similar effects on these transcripts were noted when overexpressing DacA(D164N) (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is based on RT-qPCR measurements shown in Figure 2H.

claim: No effect of YbbR_6xH overexpression on transcript levels for euo, hctA, or omcB was measured.
source: We measured no effect of YbbR_6xH overexpression on transcript levels for euo, hctA, or omcB (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is based on RT-qPCR measurements shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Overexpression of wild-type ΔTM DacA yielded the same level of c-di-AMP as overexpression of the full-length wild-type DacA.
source: As noted in Figure 1, overexpression of wild-type ΔTM DacA yielded the same level of c-di-AMP as overexpression of the full-length wild-type DacA.
evidence: This is based on ELISA measurements of c-di-AMP levels shown in Figure 1E.

claim: C-di-AMP levels measured from chlamydiae overexpressing the mutant ΔTM DacA(D164N) were the same as the mCherry-expressing strain but reduced in chlamydiae overexpressing the full-length DacA(D164N).
source: In contrast, c-di-AMP levels measured from chlamydiae overexpressing the mutant ΔTM DacA(D164N) were the same as the mCherry-expressing strain but reduced in chlamydiae overexpressing the full-length DacA(D164N).
evidence: This is based on ELISA measurements of c-di-AMP levels shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Both ΔTM isoforms localized to the cytosol, and there were no observable differences in inclusion or bacterial morphology as compared to the uninduced control.
source: By IFA, both ΔTM isoforms localized to the cytosol, and there were no observable differences in inclusion or bacterial morphology as compared to the uninduced control (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This is based on IFA images shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: Overexpression of the ΔTM isoforms resulted in no statistical differences in IFU production or genome copy numbers.
source: Overexpression of the ΔTM isoforms resulted in no statistical differences in IFU production or genome copy numbers, and, similarly, there were no differences in transcript levels for ybbR, euo, hctA, or omcB as compared to the uninduced controls (Figure 3C–H).
evidence: This is based on IFU assays and qPCR measurements shown in Figure 3C-F.

claim: There were no differences in transcript levels for ybbR, euo, hctA, or omcB when overexpressing ΔTM isoforms as compared to the uninduced controls.
source: Overexpression of the ΔTM isoforms resulted in no statistical differences in IFU production or genome copy numbers, and, similarly, there were no differences in transcript levels for ybbR, euo, hctA, or omcB as compared to the uninduced controls (Figure 3C–H).
evidence: This is based on RT-qPCR measurements shown in Figure 3G and H.

claim: The negative impacts of DacA overexpression are linked to its membrane localization and are independent of c-di-AMP production.
source: These data indicate that the negative impacts of DacA overexpression are linked to its membrane localization and are independent of c-di-AMP production.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the observation that overexpressing membrane-localized DacA isoforms (wild-type or D164N) negatively affected growth, whereas overexpressing cytosolic ΔTM isoforms did not, regardless of c-di-AMP levels.

claim: When the knockdown system was induced, bacterial cell size was enlarged (~ twofold), but no change in inclusion area was observed as compared to that of the uninduced control.
source: When the knockdown system was induced, bacterial cell size was enlarged (~ twofold), but we observed no change in inclusion area as compared to that of the uninduced control (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on IFA images and quantification shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: In the complemented strain, the inclusion area was reduced (~ threefold) with slightly larger organisms (~1.4 fold) as compared to the uninduced control.
source: However, the inclusion area was reduced (~ threefold) with slightly larger organisms (~1.4 fold) as compared to the uninduced control (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), indicating this is not the case.
evidence: This is based on quantification shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Although genome copy numbers were the same, IFUs decreased by approximately 80% compared to that of the uninduced sample at 24 hpi in the knockdown strain.
source: Although genome copy numbers were the same, IFUs decreased by approximately 80% compared to that of the uninduced sample at 24 hpi in the knockdown strain (Figure 4C and D), suggesting more RBs are present in the sample.
evidence: This is based on IFU assays and qPCR measurements shown in Figure 4C and D.

claim: IFUs and genome copies showed an approximate twofold reduction at 24 hpi in the complemented strain.
source: IFUs and genome copies showed an approximate twofold reduction at 24 hpi in the complemented strain (Figure 4E and F).
evidence: This is based on IFU assays and qPCR measurements shown in Figure 4E and F.

claim: When dCas12 was induced in the dacA-KD strain, both dacA and ybbR transcript levels decreased.
source: When dCas12 was induced, both dacA and ybbR transcript levels decreased (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is based on RT-qPCR measurements shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Transcripts of the late genes omcB and hctA were decreased at 24 hpi in the dacA-KD strain.
source: Consistent with reduced EB yields, transcripts of the late genes omcB and hctA were decreased at 24 hpi.
evidence: This is based on RT-qPCR measurements shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Transcripts of the early gene euo were slightly elevated at 24 hpi in the dacA-KD strain.
source: In contrast, transcripts of the early gene euo were slightly elevated at 24 hpi.
evidence: This is based on RT-qPCR measurements shown in Figure 4G.

claim: DacA knockdown reduces or delays expression of late gene transcripts.
source: We have previously observed no effects on genome levels or transcription of these genes when overexpressing the dCas12 gene alone (Ouellette et al., 2021), indicating these effects are specific to dacA-KD and that dacA knockdown reduces or delays expression of late gene transcripts.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the RT-qPCR data from the dacA-KD strain and comparison to previous control experiments.

claim: For the complemented strain, both dacA and ybbR transcripts were increased compared to the dacA-KD strain.
source: For the complemented strain, both dacA and ybbR transcripts were increased compared to the dacA-KD strain (Figure 4H), and transcript levels for these genes were increased beyond the 'wild-type' uninduced control levels, again suggesting the 'complemented' strain did not return to a wild-type phenotype.
evidence: This is based on RT-qPCR measurements shown in Figure 4H.

claim: Transcripts for the early gene euo were indistinguishable to levels measured in the uninduced strain in the complemented strain.
source: Nonetheless, transcripts for the early gene euo were indistinguishable to levels measured in the uninduced strain (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is based on RT-qPCR measurements shown in Figure 4H.

claim: HctA transcripts were increased ~10 fold at 14 hpi compared to that of the uninduced sample in the complemented strain.
source: Surprisingly, hctA transcripts were increased ~10 fold at 14 hpi compared to that of the uninduced sample, and omcB transcripts were slightly, but not significantly, increased at 14 and 24 hpi (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is based on RT-qPCR measurements shown in Figure 4H.

claim: Overexpressing DacA and YbbR_6xH, with associated increases in c-di-AMP levels, may alter the timing of secondary differentiation.
source: These data suggest that overexpressing DacA and YbbR_6xH, with associated increases in c-di-AMP levels (Figure 1), may alter the timing of secondary differentiation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of increased hctA transcripts at 14 hpi in the complemented strain.

claim: DacA and YbbR_6xH colocalize at the membrane.
source: When we induced expression of the wild-type constructs, we confirmed the induction of DacA and YbbR_6xH and their colocalization at the membrane Figure 5A; Pearson correlation coefficient of 0.713±0.109 from 20 inclusions measured by JACoP Plugin of ImageJ; values near 1 indicate colocalization (Bolte and Cordelières, 2006; Dunn et al., 2011).
evidence: This is based on IFA images and colocalization analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Both proteins (DacA and YbbR) are critical for c-di-AMP synthesis based on colocalization data.
source: This is not surprising as both proteins are critical for c-di-AMP synthesis based on our c-di-AMP measurements (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is an inference based on the colocalization data and previous c-di-AMP measurements.

claim: Organism and inclusion morphology in the dacAop strain were similar to the dacA-KDcom complemented strain.
source: Organism and inclusion morphology were similar to the dacA-KDcom complemented strain (Figures 4B and 5A; Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on comparison of IFA images and quantification from Figures 4B, 5A, and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The bacterial morphology of the dacAopMut strain indicated larger organisms (~1.8 fold) in smaller inclusions (~2.5 fold) after inducing expression.
source: The bacterial morphology of the dacAopMut strain indicated larger organisms (~1.8 fold) in smaller inclusions (~2.5 fold) after inducing expression (Figure 5B; Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on IFA images and quantification shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: IFUs were reduced roughly twofold for the dacAop strain after inducing overexpression.
source: IFUs were reduced roughly twofold for the dacAop strain and 1000-fold in the dacAopMut strain after inducing overexpression (Figure 5C&E).
evidence: This is based on IFU assays shown in Figure 5C.

claim: IFUs were reduced 1000-fold in the dacAopMut strain after inducing overexpression.
source: IFUs were reduced roughly twofold for the dacAop strain and 1000-fold in the dacAopMut strain after inducing overexpression (Figure 5C&E).
evidence: This is based on IFU assays shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Genome copy data for dacAop overexpression closely phenocopied the complemented knockdown strain, showing a decrease at 24 hpi.
source: Again, the genome copy data for dacAop overexpression closely phenocopied the complemented knockdown strain, showing a decrease at 24 hpi (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is based on qPCR measurements shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Genome copy numbers for the dacAopMut strain showed a significant drop at 24 hpi after inducing expression.
source: Similarly, genome copy numbers for the dacAopMut strain showed a significant drop at 24 hpi after inducing expression (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is based on qPCR measurements shown in Figure 5F.

claim: DacA and ybbR transcripts were elevated at the timepoints assessed under inducing conditions for both the dacAop and dacAopMut strains.
source: Not surprisingly, dacA and ybbR transcripts were elevated at the timepoints assessed under inducing conditions for both the dacAop and dacAopMut strains.
evidence: This is based on RT-qPCR measurements shown in Figure 5G and H.

claim: HctA transcripts were increased over 10-fold at 14 hpi in the developmental cycle during dacAop overexpression.
source: Once again, we observed that hctA transcripts were increased over 10-fold at 14 hpi in the developmental cycle (Figure 5G), similar to what we measured for the complemented knockdown strain (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is based on RT-qPCR measurements shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Elevated c-di-AMP levels lead to increased expression of the late gene hctA at an earlier timepoint (14 hpi) in the developmental cycle.
source: These data reinforce that elevated c-di-AMP levels (Figure 1E) in these strains lead to increased expression of the late gene hctA at an earlier timepoint (14 hpi) in the developmental cycle.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the RT-qPCR data showing increased hctA transcripts at 14 hpi in strains with elevated c-di-AMP levels.

claim: Transcripts for hctA and omcB were decreased at 24 hpi in the dacAopMut strain.
source: In contrast to the c-di-AMP overproducing strains, transcripts for hctA and omcB were decreased at 24 hpi (Figure 5H).
evidence: This is based on RT-qPCR measurements shown in Figure 5H.

claim: The transcriptional results of the developmentally regulated genes in the dacAopMut strain were very similar to the dacA-KD strain.
source: The transcriptional results of the developmentally regulated genes in the dacAopMut strain were very similar to the dacA-KD strain (Figure 4G), suggesting that blocking c-di-AMP accumulation interferes with developmental cycle progression.
evidence: This is based on comparison of RT-qPCR data from Figure 5H and Figure 4G.

claim: Blocking c-di-AMP accumulation interferes with developmental cycle progression.
source: The transcriptional results of the developmentally regulated genes in the dacAopMut strain were very similar to the dacA-KD strain (Figure 4G), suggesting that blocking c-di-AMP accumulation interferes with developmental cycle progression.
evidence: This is an inference based on the similarity of transcriptional profiles between dacAopMut and dacA-KD strains.

claim: Many late genes were evident in the upregulated quadrant for the dacAop strain in the RNA sequencing volcano plot.
source: Of note, many late genes were evident in the upregulated quadrant for the dacAop strain whereas these genes were present in the downregulated quadrant for the dacA-KD strain.
evidence: This is based on the RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Late genes were present in the downregulated quadrant for the dacA-KD strain in the RNA sequencing volcano plot.
source: Of note, many late genes were evident in the upregulated quadrant for the dacAop strain whereas these genes were present in the downregulated quadrant for the dacA-KD strain.
evidence: This is based on the RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 6.

claim: All canonical late genes showed an increase in expression after c-di-AMP production was induced in the dacAop strain.
source: Consistent with our RT-qPCR data, we observed that all canonical late genes, as well as all the other genes listed in these categories, showed an increase in expression after c-di-AMP production was induced.
evidence: This is based on the RNA sequencing data shown in Table 1 and Supplementary file 2.

claim: All canonical late genes showed a decrease in expression under conditions where c-di-AMP production was impaired in the dacA-KD strain.
source: In contrast, all the genes, and particularly the canonical late genes, showed a decrease in expression under conditions where c-di-AMP production was impaired.
evidence: This is based on the RNA sequencing data shown in Table 1 and Supplementary file 2.

claim: RNA sequencing data confirm the direct influence of c-di-AMP on expression of genes related to secondary differentiation.
source: Overall, these RNA sequencing data confirm the direct influence of c-di-AMP on expression of genes related to secondary differentiation.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the comprehensive RNA sequencing data showing differential expression of late genes in strains with altered c-di-AMP levels.

claim: Higher EB yields were measured at 18 and 20 hpi during dacAop overexpression that quickly plateaued by 24 hpi.
source: Consistent with the transcriptional data, we measured higher EB yields at 18 and 20 hpi during dacAop overexpression that quickly plateaued by 24 hpi (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is based on IFU assays shown in Figure 7A.

claim: When c-di-AMP accumulation was blocked by reducing the expression of DacA and YbbR (dacA-KD), delayed EB production was observed.
source: Conversely, when c-di-AMP accumulation was blocked by reducing the expression of DacA and YbbR (dacA-KD), we observed delayed EB production (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is based on IFU assays shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Lower EB yields were measured when c-di-AMP levels were decreased by overexpression of the DacA(D164N) isoform and YbbR (dacAopMut).
source: We also measured lower EB yields when c-di-AMP levels were decreased by overexpression of the DacA(D164N) isoform and YbbR (dacAopMut; Figure 7C).
evidence: This is based on IFU assays shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Earlier production of c-di-AMP results in earlier production of EBs.
source: From these data, we conclude that earlier production of c-di-AMP results in earlier production of EBs.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the IFU data showing earlier EB production in strains with elevated c-di-AMP levels.

claim: This is the first study to identify and provide experimental evidence for a signaling factor involved in differentiation of an obligate intracellular bacterium.
source: To our knowledge, this is the first study to identify and provide experimental evidence for a signaling factor involved in differentiation of an obligate intracellular bacterium.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the study based on the authors' knowledge of the literature.

claim: Chlamydia lacks orthologs of proteins that have been characterized in other bacterial systems to bind c-di-AMP.
source: This is not readily apparent because Chlamydia lacks orthologs of proteins that have been characterized in other bacterial systems to bind c-di-AMP.
evidence: This is based on genomic analysis of Chlamydia.

claim: Changes in K+ levels affect the chlamydial developmental cycle.
source: However, a recent study suggested that changes in K+ levels affect the chlamydial developmental cycle (Andrew et al., 2021).
evidence: This is based on the citation to Andrew et al., 2021.

claim: C-di-AMP may function as a K+ homeostasis coordinator in Chlamydia through as-yet unknown pathways.
source: Therefore, c-di-AMP may function as a K+ homeostasis coordinator in Chlamydia through as-yet unknown pathways.
evidence: This is speculation based on the known function of c-di-AMP in other bacteria and the observation that K+ levels affect chlamydial development.

claim: In S. aureus, DacA activity is inhibited by interacting with GlmM (phosphoglucosamine mutase).
source: In regard to the latter possibility, in S. aureus, DacA activity is inhibited by interacting with GlmM (phosphoglucosamine mutase) (Tosi et al., 2019).
evidence: This is based on the citation to Tosi et al., 2019.

claim: GlmM produces UDP-GlcNAc that is a precursor in both peptidoglycan and LPS synthesis.
source: GlmM produces UDP-GlcNAc that is a precursor in both peptidoglycan and LPS synthesis.
evidence: This is established biochemical knowledge.

claim: DacA and YbbR localization was not associated with the division septum.
source: However, their localization was not associated with the division septum (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on IFA images shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: No interaction between DacA and GlmM was detected using the Bacterial Adenylate Cyclase-based Two-Hybrid (BACTH) system.
source: In addition, we did not detect an interaction between DacA and GlmM using the Bacterial Adenylate Cyclase-based Two-Hybrid (BACTH) system (data not shown), and the chlamydial GlmM lacks the residues required for DacA interaction.
evidence: This is based on experimental data from the BACTH system.

claim: The chlamydial GlmM lacks the residues required for DacA interaction.
source: In addition, we did not detect an interaction between DacA and GlmM using the Bacterial Adenylate Cyclase-based Two-Hybrid (BACTH) system (data not shown), and the chlamydial GlmM lacks the residues required for DacA interaction.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis of chlamydial GlmM.

claim: DacA and YbbR are unlikely to directly impact cell division.
source: Therefore, we conclude that DacA and YbbR are unlikely to directly impact cell division.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the lack of septal localization and lack of interaction with GlmM.

claim: Based on the cell morphological changes in DacA overexpression, a function for c-di-AMP on cell wall metabolism cannot be excluded.
source: However, based on the cell morphological changes in DacA overexpression, we cannot exclude a function for c-di-AMP on cell wall metabolism.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observed morphological changes.

claim: DacA-ybbR transcripts peak during the RB phase of growth, similar to most genes in Chlamydia.
source: Our transcript analyses indicate that dacA-ybbR transcripts peak during the RB phase of growth, similar to most genes in Chlamydia.
evidence: This is based on the RT-qPCR data presented in the study.

claim: C-di-AMP production depletes ATP levels, which then reduce σ66 activity.
source: One possibility not easily tested due to the obligate intracellular nature of Chlamydia is that c-di-AMP production depletes ATP levels, which then reduce σ66 activity as described above.
evidence: This is speculation about a possible mechanism linking c-di-AMP to transcriptional regulation.

claim: YbbR is necessary to activate DacA function since expressing membrane-localized or ΔTM isoforms of DacA alone only modestly increased c-di-AMP levels.
source: Our data indicate YbbR is necessary to activate DacA function since expressing membrane-localized or ΔTM isoforms of DacA alone only modestly increased c-di-AMP levels (Figure 1E).
evidence: This conclusion is based on the c-di-AMP measurements showing that co-expression of DacA and YbbR results in much higher c-di-AMP levels than DacA alone.

claim: Overexpressing DacA alone negatively impacted chlamydial growth, suggesting that the balance between DacA and YbbR levels is important, with YbbR being the limiting factor for c-di-AMP production.
source: However, overexpressing DacA alone did negatively impact chlamydial growth, suggesting that the balance between DacA and YbbR levels is important, with YbbR being the limiting factor for c-di-AMP production.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that overexpressing DacA alone negatively affects growth but does not dramatically increase c-di-AMP levels.

claim: Too much DacA insertion into the membrane without binding to YbbR may disrupt the membrane biology of the RB.
source: For example, too much DacA insertion into the membrane without binding to YbbR may disrupt the membrane biology of the RB.
evidence: This is speculation about why overexpressing DacA alone negatively affects growth.

claim: No detrimental effects of overexpressing ΔTM isoforms of either wild-type or mutant (D164N) DacA were observed.
source: This is supported by the fact that we observed no detrimental effects of overexpressing ΔTM isoforms of either wild-type or mutant (D164N) DacA.
evidence: This is based on the data from Figure 3 showing no effects on growth or development when overexpressing ΔTM DacA isoforms.

claim: Overexpressing ΔTMDacA(D164N) did not alter c-di-AMP levels.
source: Indeed, overexpressing ΔTMDacA(D164N) did not alter c-di-AMP levels.
evidence: This is based on the c-di-AMP measurements shown in Figure 1E.

claim: YbbR itself may be a target for regulation.
source: Therefore, YbbR itself may be a target for regulation.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation that YbbR is the limiting factor for c-di-AMP production.

claim: YbbR may be degraded by proteases such as the inner membrane-associated FtsH or the periplasmic proteases HtrA or Tsp.
source: As a monotopic transmembrane protein, YbbR may be degraded by proteases such as the inner membrane-associated FtsH or the periplasmic proteases HtrA or Tsp.
evidence: This is speculation about possible mechanisms for regulating YbbR levels.

claim: DacA may interact with other membrane proteins, and overexpressing it alone may impair the function of this binding partner(s), resulting in the observed phenotypes.
source: Alternatively, DacA may interact with other membrane proteins, and overexpressing it alone may impair the function of this binding partner(s), resulting in the observed phenotypes.
evidence: This is speculation about alternative mechanisms for the negative effects of DacA overexpression.

claim: The mutant DacA(D164N) isoform acts as a dominant negative by binding and/or interfering with the wild-type DacA or by titrating away YbbR from the wild-type DacA.
source: These experiments were conducted in the presence of the chromosomally expressed copy of DacA, and we suggest that the mutant isoform acts as a dominant negative by binding and/or interfering with the wild-type DacA or by titrating away YbbR from the wild-type DacA.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that overexpressing DacA(D164N) blocks c-di-AMP production even in the presence of wild-type DacA.

claim: Overexpressing the ΔTMDacA(D164N) isoform had no impact on c-di-AMP levels or chlamydial growth.
source: This is also supported by the fact that overexpressing the ΔTMDacA(D164N) isoform had no impact on c-di-AMP levels or chlamydial growth.
evidence: This is based on the data from Figures 1E and 3 showing no effects when overexpressing ΔTMDacA(D164N).

claim: Knocking down dacA-ybbR transcripts will reduce, but not completely eliminate, DacA and YbbR proteins, which may result in residual c-di-AMP levels as compared to overexpressing the DacA mutant.
source: In contrast, knocking down dacA-ybbR transcripts will reduce, but not completely eliminate, DacA and YbbR proteins, which may result in residual c-di-AMP levels as compared to overexpressing the DacA mutant (either alone or with YbbR in dacAopMut) as well as the phenotypic differences between these strains.
evidence: This is an inference to explain the differences between the dacA-KD and dacAopMut strains.

claim: The data are clear in linking increased c-di-AMP levels to chlamydial developmental progression.
source: However, our data are clear in linking increased c-di-AMP levels to chlamydial developmental progression.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main finding of the study.

claim: This is the first time c-di-AMP has been described as a checkpoint in chlamydial development.
source: Even though diverse functions of c-di-AMP in other bacteria have been reported previously, this is the first time c-di-AMP has been described as a checkpoint in chlamydial development.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the study.

claim: The levels of c-di-AMP may act as a de facto means for monitoring the bacterial population within the inclusion or for their overall developmental status.
source: It is possible that the levels of c-di-AMP act as a de facto means for monitoring the bacterial population within the inclusion or for their overall developmental status.
evidence: This is speculation about the broader function of c-di-AMP in Chlamydia.

claim: C. trachomatis lacks homologues of genes related to quorum sensing.
source: However, C. trachomatis lacks homologues of genes related to quorum sensing (Stephens et al., 1998).
evidence: This is based on genomic analysis of C. trachomatis supported by the citation to Stephens et al., 1998.

claim: Secondary differentiation occurs asynchronously.
source: In addition, secondary differentiation occurs asynchronously, and this feature is different from a quorum sensing mechanism.
evidence: This is a known characteristic of chlamydial development.

claim: The model accounts for the asynchronicity of secondary differentiation.
source: Our model accounts for the asynchronicity of secondary differentiation.
evidence: This is a claim about the explanatory power of the proposed model.

claim: As RBs accumulate c-di-AMP and divide, it is likely the c-di-AMP will be distributed unevenly between the mother and daughter cells since Chlamydia divides through an asymmetric budding mechanism.
source: As RBs accumulate c-di-AMP and divide, it is likely the c-di-AMP will be distributed unevenly between the mother and daughter cells since Chlamydia divides through an asymmetric budding mechanism (Abdelrahman et al., 2016; Figure 8).
evidence: This is an inference based on the known asymmetric division mechanism of Chlamydia and the properties of c-di-AMP as a diffusible molecule.

claim: Uneven distribution of c-di-AMP will lead to two cells with different levels of c-di-AMP, one of which may then accumulate enough c-di-AMP to trigger secondary differentiation while the other continues to divide.
source: This will lead to two cells with different levels of c-di-AMP, one of which may then accumulate enough c-di-AMP to trigger secondary differentiation while the other continues to divide (Figure 8).
evidence: This is an inference based on the proposed model of c-di-AMP distribution during division.

claim: A population of division-competent RBs is maintained throughout the developmental cycle.
source: This is consistent with a recent model proposing that a population of division-competent RBs is maintained throughout the developmental cycle (Chiarelli et al., 2023).
evidence: This is based on the citation to Chiarelli et al., 2023.

claim: Similar uneven distribution of post-translational factors between asymmetrically dividing mother and daughter cells would also impact other recently described signals for differentiation, including the levels of ClpC protein or overall redox via AhpC antioxidant levels.
source: Similar uneven distribution of post-translational factors between asymmetrically dividing mother and daughter cells would also impact other recently described signals for differentiation, including the levels of ClpC protein or overall redox via AhpC antioxidant levels (Jensen et al., 2025; Singh and Ouellette, 2025).
evidence: This is an inference connecting the proposed model to other recently described mechanisms of differentiation.

claim: The threshold level of c-di-AMP necessary to trigger secondary differentiation in the culture conditions is greater than 1000 pg/mL and less than 2000 pg/mL.
source: We can also directly conclude from our experiments that the threshold level of c-di-AMP necessary to trigger secondary differentiation in our culture conditions is greater than 1000 pg/mL and less than 2000 pg/mL.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the c-di-AMP measurements showing that 1000 pg/mL at 16 hpi in the DacA-overexpressing strain did not trigger differentiation, whereas ~2000 pg/mL at 24 hpi in the control strain is associated with EB production.
